chapters.category: Ethiopic textual tradition • Modern English research translation
chapters.title: Chapter 6 — Covenant, Blood, and Sacred Time
chapters.sourceNote: Translated afresh into clear modern English from the earliest complete primary-language witness responsibly available for this chapter: the Ethiopic (Geʽez) text preserved in manuscripts A–D and printed as Jubilees 6:1–38 on text pages 22–25 of R. H. Charles’s 1895 critical edition, The Ethiopic Version of the Hebrew Book of Jubilees. No surviving Hebrew or Greek fragment preserving wording from Jubilees 6 was located. Although the fifth-century Latin codex originally contained this chapter, its corresponding leaves are not extant and supply no text. No modern English translation was used as the translation base, no commentary was used as Scripture, and no wording absent from the primary witness was supplied.

verses.text: On the new moon of the third month, Noah came out from the ark and built an altar on that mountain.
verses.study: Noah’s first recorded act after leaving the ark is worship. The new beginning is marked by an altar and by time deliberately remembered.
crossReferences: Genesis 8:18–20 — Noah leaves the ark and builds an altar
Exodus 20:24 — an altar becomes a place for offerings before God

verses.text: He made atonement for the earth. He took a young goat and, with its blood, made atonement for all the earth’s guilt, because everything that had been upon it was destroyed except those who were in the ark with Noah.
verses.study: The sacrifice acknowledges that the renewed earth still bears the history of guilt and judgment. Preservation in the ark does not make atonement unnecessary.
crossReferences: Leviticus 17:11 — sacrificial blood is given for making atonement
Genesis 7:21–23 — life outside the ark perishes in the flood

verses.text: He put its fat upon the altar. Then he took an ox, a goat, a sheep, young goats, salt, a turtledove, and a young pigeon, and offered a burnt offering on the altar. He poured over it a grain offering mixed with oil, sprinkled wine upon it, and placed frankincense over everything. He caused a pleasing aroma to rise, acceptable before the Lord.
verses.study: Noah’s offering gathers animals, grain, oil, wine, salt, and incense into an act of whole devotion. The accepted aroma expresses God’s favorable reception of worship offered according to his provision.
crossReferences: Genesis 8:20–21 — the Lord receives the pleasing aroma of Noah’s offering
Leviticus 2:1–2, 13 — grain, oil, frankincense, and salt accompany an offering

verses.text: The Lord smelled the pleasing aroma and made a covenant with Noah: never again would there be a flood to destroy the earth. Throughout all the earth’s days, seedtime and harvest, cold and heat, summer and winter, day and night would never cease or change their appointed order.
verses.study: God binds the stability of ordinary creation to covenant mercy. The recurring seasons testify that judgment has not cancelled his sustaining purpose for the earth.
crossReferences: Genesis 8:21–22 — the cycles of the earth are promised continuing order
Jeremiah 33:20–21 — the fixed covenant with day and night displays God’s faithfulness

verses.text: ‘As for you, be fruitful and multiply upon the earth; increase upon it and become a blessing within it. I will put fear and dread of you upon everything on the earth and in the sea.
verses.study: Humanity receives again the commission to fill the earth, now in a world where creatures fear human rule. Fruitfulness remains a gift meant to carry blessing.
crossReferences: Genesis 9:1–2 — Noah’s family receives fruitfulness and authority after the flood
Genesis 1:28 — humanity is commissioned to multiply and govern creaturely life

verses.text: Look, I have given you every land animal, every winged creature, everything that moves upon the earth, and the fish in the waters. Everything is given to you for food. Just as I gave you the green plants, I have given you everything to eat.
verses.study: God grants food from animal life as he had granted plants. The gift remains governed by the limits that immediately follow.
crossReferences: Genesis 9:3 — moving creatures are given for food as the plants were
1 Timothy 4:4–5 — created food is received with thanksgiving under God’s word

verses.text: But you must not eat flesh with its life, that is, with its blood, because the life of all flesh is in the blood. I will require an account for your lifeblood. I will require human blood from every animal and from every person; from each man I will require the life of his brother.
verses.study: Permission to eat is bounded by reverence for life, which belongs to God. Blood represents life and therefore cannot be treated as ordinary food or shed without accountability.
crossReferences: Genesis 9:4–5 — blood is forbidden as food and lifeblood is required
Leviticus 17:10–14 — the life of flesh is in its blood

verses.text: Whoever sheds human blood, by a human being shall his blood be shed, because God made humanity in his own image.
verses.study: Human life carries unique dignity because it bears God’s image. The prohibition of murder rests not on social usefulness but on the Creator’s mark in every person.
crossReferences: Genesis 9:6 — the image of God grounds judgment for bloodshed
James 3:9 — human beings are made in God’s likeness

verses.text: As for you, be fruitful, multiply upon the earth, and increase throughout it.’
verses.study: The renewed command follows the protection of life. Multiplication is to proceed within a covenant order that restrains violence.
crossReferences: Genesis 9:7 — Noah’s family is told to multiply abundantly
Psalm 115:14–15 — blessing is invoked upon a people and their children

verses.text: Noah and his sons swore that they would not consume blood found in any flesh. In this month Noah made a covenant before the Lord God forever, throughout all the earth’s generations.
verses.study: Noah’s household answers divine command with a binding promise. The chapter connects obedience concerning blood with covenant continuity across generations.
crossReferences: Genesis 9:8–17 — God establishes his covenant with Noah and his descendants
Deuteronomy 12:23 — Israel is firmly commanded not to eat the blood

verses.text: For this reason he told you to make a covenant with Israel’s children in this month upon the mountain, with an oath, and to sprinkle blood upon them because of all the words of the covenant that the Lord made with them forever.
verses.study: The narrator links Noah’s covenant month with Israel’s covenant at the mountain. Sprinkled blood solemnly binds the people to the words they have received.
crossReferences: Exodus 24:3–8 — covenant words are affirmed and blood is sprinkled upon the people
Hebrews 9:18–20 — the first covenant is inaugurated with blood

verses.text: This testimony is written concerning you so that you may always observe it: throughout all the earth’s days you must never eat the blood of any animal, bird, or livestock. Whoever eats the blood of an animal, livestock, or bird shall be uprooted from the earth, both that person and his offspring.
verses.study: The blood command is presented as a lasting written testimony, not a passing custom. Its severe sanction underscores that life may not be consumed as though it belonged to humanity.
crossReferences: Leviticus 7:26–27 — anyone who eats blood is cut off from the people
Leviticus 17:14 — blood must not be eaten because it is the life of every creature

verses.text: Command Israel’s children not to eat blood, so that their names and their offspring may remain continually before the Lord our God.
verses.study: Abstaining from blood is joined to continued life before God. Covenant obedience honors the giver of life and preserves communal identity.
crossReferences: Deuteronomy 12:25 — abstaining from blood is connected with well-being for descendants
Psalm 69:28 — names remaining in the book of life portray enduring standing before God

verses.text: This law has no limit of days, for it is established forever. They must observe it throughout their generations, so that they may continue to make supplication for you with blood at the altar every day. Morning and evening they shall seek forgiveness for you continually before the Lord, so that you may keep this command and not be uprooted.
verses.study: Blood is forbidden as food yet appointed for sacrificial supplication. Daily worship teaches that atonement is God’s provision and must not be confused with human consumption.
crossReferences: Exodus 29:38–42 — offerings are presented morning and evening continually
Leviticus 17:11 — God assigns blood to the altar for atonement

verses.text: He gave Noah and his sons a sign that there would never again be a flood over the earth.
verses.study: The covenant promise is joined to a visible sign. God provides reassurance for the generations that live under the memory of judgment.
crossReferences: Genesis 9:11–13 — the covenant sign accompanies the promise against another flood
Isaiah 54:9 — the waters of Noah become the pattern for a sworn promise of mercy

verses.text: He placed his bow in the cloud as the sign of the eternal covenant that the waters of a flood would never again cover the earth to destroy it throughout all the earth’s days.
verses.study: The bow in the cloud turns the storm itself into a reminder of restraint. The covenant sign points to God’s enduring mercy toward the whole earth.
crossReferences: Genesis 9:13–16 — the bow in the cloud marks the everlasting covenant
Ezekiel 1:28 — the appearance of a rainbow surrounds a vision of divine glory

verses.text: Therefore it is ordained and written on the heavenly tablets that the Feast of Weeks must be celebrated in this month, once each year, to renew the covenant every year.
verses.study: Annual worship renews communal remembrance of the covenant. Sacred time trains each generation to receive God’s promise as a present obligation.
crossReferences: Leviticus 23:15–21 — the Feast of Weeks is observed at its appointed time
Deuteronomy 16:9–12 — Israel celebrates Weeks and remembers deliverance

verses.text: This entire feast was celebrated in heaven from the day of creation until Noah’s time: twenty-six jubilees and five weeks of years. Noah and his sons observed it for seven jubilees and one week of years, until the day Noah died. From Noah’s death his sons abandoned it until Abraham’s days, and they ate blood.
verses.study: The chapter portrays the feast as belonging to creation’s heavenly order before Israel’s later observance. Neglect of the feast is paired with neglect of the command concerning blood.
crossReferences: Genesis 9:28–29 — Noah’s life continues after the flood and then ends
Nehemiah 9:13–17 — received commandments can be abandoned by later generations

verses.text: Abraham observed it, and Isaac, Jacob, and Jacob’s children observed it until your days. In your days Israel’s children forgot it, until I renewed it for them on this mountain.
verses.study: Faithful remembrance passes through the patriarchs but is later lost and restored. Sinai is presented as renewal as well as revelation.
crossReferences: Genesis 26:5 — Abraham keeps God’s charge, commandments, statutes, and laws
Exodus 19:1–6 — Israel comes to the mountain and receives the covenant call

verses.text: Command Israel’s children to observe this feast throughout their generations as a statute for them. On one day each year, in this month, they must celebrate the feast.
verses.study: The command gives a recurring day to covenant memory. Observance must continue beyond the founding generation.
crossReferences: Leviticus 23:21 — the feast is a lasting statute throughout generations
Numbers 28:26 — the day of firstfruits is kept as a sacred assembly

verses.text: For it is the Feast of Weeks and the Feast of Firstfruits. This feast has a twofold character and a double witness. Celebrate it according to what is written and engraved concerning it.
verses.study: Two names join counted weeks with harvest firstfruits. The feast binds time and provision together in written testimony.
crossReferences: Exodus 34:22 — the Feast of Weeks is identified with the firstfruits of wheat harvest
Deuteronomy 16:10 — the Feast of Weeks follows a counted period and is celebrated with giving

verses.text: I have written in the book of the first law, in what I wrote for you, that you must celebrate it at its appointed time one day each year. I explained its sacrifices to you so that Israel’s children may remember and celebrate it throughout their generations, in this month, one day every year.
verses.study: Written instruction fixes both the feast’s time and its offerings. Remembering is enacted through obedient worship rather than recollection alone.
crossReferences: Leviticus 23:15–20 — the appointed count and sacrifices of Weeks are specified
Numbers 28:26–31 — offerings for the day of firstfruits are prescribed

verses.text: The new moons of the first, fourth, seventh, and tenth months are days of remembrance and days marking the seasons in the four divisions of the year. These are written and ordained as a testimony forever.
verses.study: Four remembered new moons mark the year’s ordered divisions. The calendar is treated as testimony to a creation governed by appointed times.
crossReferences: Genesis 1:14 — the heavenly lights mark signs, seasons, days, and years
1 Chronicles 23:31 — offerings accompany new moons and appointed festivals

verses.text: Noah established them for himself as feasts throughout eternal generations, and by them they became a memorial for him.
verses.study: Noah answers deliverance by ordering remembrance. Repeated feast days keep acts of judgment and mercy from fading into unmarked history.
crossReferences: Exodus 12:14 — a saving act is kept as a memorial feast throughout generations
Psalm 105:5 — God’s people are called to remember his wonders and judgments

verses.text: On the new moon of the first month he had been told to make an ark for himself. On that date the earth also became dry, and he opened the ark and saw the land.
verses.study: The same calendar date gathers warning and restored sight of dry land. God’s command to prepare and his completion of deliverance frame the remembered day.
crossReferences: Genesis 6:13–14 — Noah is commanded to make the ark
Genesis 8:13 — on the first day of the first month Noah sees that the ground is dry

verses.text: On the new moon of the fourth month the mouths of the depths of the abyss beneath were closed. On the new moon of the seventh month all the mouths of the earth’s abysses were opened, and the waters began to descend into them.
verses.study: The remembered dates trace God’s control over the waters below. The deep that helped overwhelm the world is also commanded to receive the floodwaters back.
crossReferences: Genesis 8:1–2 — the fountains of the deep are closed and the waters recede
Psalm 104:7–9 — God rebukes the waters and assigns their boundary

verses.text: On the new moon of the tenth month the mountain tops appeared, and Noah rejoiced.
verses.study: The first visible heights signal that the submerged world is returning. Joy arises when God’s restoration becomes visible after prolonged waiting.
crossReferences: Genesis 8:5 — the mountain tops appear in the tenth month
Psalm 30:5 — sorrow gives way to joy under God’s favor

verses.text: For this reason Noah established these days for himself as feasts of remembrance forever, and so they are ordained.
verses.study: The calendar turns personal deliverance into enduring communal memory. Ordained celebration gives later generations a share in remembered mercy.
crossReferences: Deuteronomy 8:2 — Israel is commanded to remember the whole way of deliverance
Esther 9:27–28 — days of rescue are established for annual remembrance

verses.text: They placed them on the heavenly tablets. Each division has thirteen weeks, and their memorial passes from one division to the next: from the first to the second, from the second to the third, and from the third to the fourth.
verses.study: The four equal divisions present the year as a coherent ordered whole. The heavenly tablets ground the calendar in testimony beyond changing human custom.
crossReferences: Daniel 7:10 — heavenly books stand open before the divine court
Ecclesiastes 3:1 — every matter has its appointed season

verses.text: All the days governed by the command will be fifty-two weeks of days, and together they make a complete year.
verses.study: Fifty-two full weeks unite weekly rhythm with the annual cycle. The year’s completeness is measured through uninterrupted sevens.
crossReferences: Leviticus 23:15–16 — complete weeks are counted to an appointed feast
Genesis 2:2–3 — the seven-day pattern is rooted in creation

verses.text: Thus it is engraved and ordained on the heavenly tablets. They must not neglect its observance for even a single year, but must keep it from year to year.
verses.study: The command is both fixed and recurring. Faithfulness in sacred time requires sustained observance rather than occasional recovery.
crossReferences: Deuteronomy 16:16 — Israel appears before the Lord at recurring annual feasts
Psalm 119:89–91 — God’s word and created order remain established

verses.text: Command Israel’s children to observe the years according to this reckoning: three hundred sixty-four days make a complete year. They must not disturb its time, its days, or its feasts, because everything will occur in them according to their testimony. They will neither omit a day nor displace a feast.
verses.study: The chapter insists that worship remain aligned with its prescribed calendar. Accurate reckoning protects the relation among days, seasons, and feasts.
crossReferences: Leviticus 23:4 — appointed feasts are proclaimed at their proper times
Numbers 9:2–3 — Passover is kept at its appointed time according to its statutes

verses.text: But if they neglect them and do not observe them according to his command, they will disturb all their seasons. The years will be displaced from this order, the appointed times and years will shift, and they will neglect their ordinances.
verses.study: Calendar disorder becomes covenant disorder when appointed worship is abandoned. Neglect compounds as displaced seasons obscure the commands tied to them.
crossReferences: Hosea 2:11 — feasts, new moons, and Sabbaths can cease under covenant judgment
Daniel 7:25 — changing appointed times is portrayed as an act of rebellion

verses.text: All Israel’s children will forget and will no longer find the path of the years. They will forget the new moons, appointed seasons, and Sabbaths, and they will go astray concerning the entire order of the years.
verses.study: Forgetting sacred time is described as losing a path. The calendar serves remembrance only when the people continue walking in its ordered practices.
crossReferences: Ezekiel 22:26 — failure to distinguish holy from common corrupts worship
Nehemiah 13:17–18 — neglect of the Sabbath repeats earlier unfaithfulness

verses.text: For I know, and from now on I will declare it to you—not from my own understanding, because the book is written before me. The division of days is ordained on the heavenly tablets, so that they do not forget the covenant feasts and begin walking according to the feasts of the nations, following their error and ignorance.
verses.study: The angelic speaker grounds the warning in a written heavenly record, not private speculation. Israel’s calendar is meant to guard covenant identity from assimilation.
crossReferences: Exodus 23:13 — Israel must not invoke the gods of surrounding peoples
Deuteronomy 12:29–31 — Israel must not adopt the nations’ forms of worship

verses.text: There will be people who carefully observe the moon, but it disrupts the seasons and advances from year to year by ten days.
verses.study: Zealous observation can still misalign worship if its measure conflicts with the chapter’s ordained reckoning. Precision alone is not faithfulness; the governing testimony matters.
crossReferences: Psalm 104:19 — the moon marks appointed times within God’s creation
Colossians 2:16 — disputes over festivals and new moons must not replace the substance of faithfulness

verses.text: Because of this, years will come upon them in which they disturb the order. They will make a day of testimony detestable and call an unclean day a feast. They will confuse all the days—the holy with the unclean and the unclean with the holy—because they will go astray concerning the months, Sabbaths, feasts, and jubilees.
verses.study: Misordered time produces reversed moral and liturgical judgments. The warning reaches beyond arithmetic to the danger of calling holy what is unclean and unclean what is holy.
crossReferences: Isaiah 5:20 — woe falls on those who reverse good and evil
Ezekiel 44:23 — priests must teach the difference between holy and common, clean and unclean

verses.text: Therefore I command you and testify to you, so that you may testify to them. After your death your children will cause disorder and will not make the year three hundred sixty-four days only. Because of this they will go astray concerning the new moons, appointed seasons, Sabbaths, and festivals, and they will eat every kind of blood with every kind of flesh.
verses.study: The chapter closes by joining calendar unfaithfulness with the blood prohibition from its opening covenant. Moses must transmit the warning because later disorder will touch both worship and reverence for life.
crossReferences: Deuteronomy 31:27–29 — Moses warns that corruption will follow after his death
Leviticus 19:26, 30 — abstaining from blood and keeping Sabbaths stand together in covenant obedience

explanation.heading: Chapter teaching and context
paragraphs: Chapter 6 begins with Noah’s worship after the flood. His offering acknowledges the earth’s guilt, and God answers with a covenant that preserves the ordered rhythms of creation. The promise does not remove moral limits: humanity may receive animal life as food, but blood remains sacred because it represents life, and human bloodshed is judged because every person bears God’s image.

The chapter connects Noah’s covenant with Israel’s covenant at Sinai. Both are marked by oath and blood, while the prohibition against consuming blood distinguishes sacrificial atonement from food. Blood is reserved for the altar’s God-given ministry of supplication; it may not be consumed as though life belonged to the worshiper.

The Feast of Weeks renews covenant remembrance in the third month. The text traces its observance from heaven and Noah through Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob to Sinai, portraying sacred celebration as recovered testimony. Firstfruits, counted weeks, and annual sacrifice join gratitude for provision with fidelity to the covenant.

The final section treats the calendar as a moral discipline of remembrance. Four seasonal markers divide a 364-day year into fifty-two complete weeks. The chapter warns that losing this order will displace feasts, blur holy and unclean days, and accompany disregard for the command concerning blood. Its theological concern is faithful transmission: God’s people must receive, remember, and hand on the appointed patterns that honor creation, covenant, worship, and life.

crossReferences: Genesis 8:18–22 — Noah leaves the ark, offers sacrifice, and receives the promise of ordered seasons
Genesis 9:1–17 — fruitfulness, blood, the divine image, and the covenant sign
Exodus 24:1–11 — Israel’s covenant at the mountain is ratified with blood
Leviticus 17:10–14 — blood is reserved because it contains the life of flesh
Leviticus 23:15–21 — the Feast of Weeks and firstfruits are kept at their appointed time
Numbers 28:26–31 — sacrifices are prescribed for the day of firstfruits
Deuteronomy 12:20–28 — meat may be eaten but blood must be poured out
Deuteronomy 16:9–12 — counted weeks lead to a feast of grateful remembrance
Psalm 104:19 — created lights serve appointed times
Isaiah 5:20 — moral disorder reverses holy distinctions
Ezekiel 44:23 — God’s servants distinguish holy from common and clean from unclean
Hebrews 9:18–22 — covenant inauguration and cleansing are associated with blood
